newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway's central bank raises key interest rates.
newsitem.headline: Norway's central bank raises key interest rates.

text.p: Norway's central bank said on Wednesday it was raising its key interest rates by 0.25 percentage points in response to recent developments in money and foreign exchange markets.

The bank increased its deposit rate, the credit rate, to 3.50 percent from 3.25 percent. The overnight lending rate, charged to commercial and savings banks, was raised to 5.50 percent from 5.25 percent.
The rise is effective from July 16, Norges Bank said in a statement.

"Central Bank governor Kjell Storvik points out that the operational goal for monetary and exchange rate policy is a stable exchange rate against European currencies and that the decision was made in response to recent developments in money and foreign exchange markets," it said.
In January the bank cut both interest rates twice in two days after massive intervention in the foreign exchange market failed to dampen a sharp appreciation in the crown.
Since the last rate cuts the crown has fallen more than seven percent against the inverse European Currency Unit (ECU) index.
Norges Bank at the end of July began announcing a series of fixed interest rates for its fixed-term deposits, which usually are carried out through ordinary auction.

This has pushed up short-term money market rates more than 65 basis points. At 0730 GMT, shortly after the bank's rate announcement, the three-month swap rate stood at 4.16 percent compared with 4.14 percent at 1400 GMT on Tuesday. The crown, meanwhile was at 103.26 against the ECU index versus 103.72.
"This is not surprising. The rate rise is a wise decision taking into account the Norwegian economic cycle at present," Eirik Larsen, chief forex analyst at Den norske Bank.
"It is an important signal that low rates cannot last for ever, but I do not think this is the start of a new cycle of rate hikes, it is more a symbolic signal," Larsen said.
